I thought it was interesting, especially the writer's point about body control bringing back a sense of awareness that you kind of "tune out" when playing a game. In real life we have a sense called "proprioception", which is our awareness of our body position even when it's not visible to us. In video games we don't have a sense of proprioception, so it's interesting to see how games mimic that sense of body position awareness, and which games don't bother with it at all.

My problem is that it repurposes the E and Q keys, I like them to be use and inventory respectively. I don't think I've ever effectively used lean in any game.
Yeah, I know what you mean. Micro managing your character's movement to that degree means juggling an extra level of input that just isn't worth it to me.

It's a very interesting concept but its not without its issues.

With a mouse + keyboard control setup, typically, the mechanic is intended for the Q and E keys, which has two problems: For one, those are awkward to hold down for an extended period of time because that's not what you usually do in an FPS and doing so makes it extremely difficult / annoying to strafe at the same time, which brings me to the next point: Unless you have analog control over the amount of leaning, which you typically don't have with digital input actions like from a keyboard, you will have a fixed amount of leaning that a single button press will cause. To carefully lean / move around a corner like you would in real life, you would require either analog control over the amount of lean, or, with a fixed amount of leaning, a strafing movement on top of that, which, again, is difficult if you have to hold down Q or E and then need to hold A or D in addition to that. Toggle control kind of solves this but having to press a key to go out of lean feels less intuitive than just releasing a key again and it's more clumsy, especially if you have to do so quickly. You could use keys on the mouse but most people typically have a 5-button mouse and various typical FPS control functions mapped to them already, so you'll have a hard time sacrificing two mouse buttons for leaning and finding other keys to compensate.

Paradoxically, leaning in FPS games can probably best achieved with a gamepad, but then precision aiming with a gamepad is, with current technology (and probably will always be) so inferior to kb + m aiming that it's a bit of a moot point (the popularity of FPS games on consoles in the last decade notwithstanding).

The article also mentions ARMA which is a great example of the mechanic's ups and downs: On the one hand, it's probably the most complex implementation offering the biggest degree of freedom for stances ever implemented in an FPS, but on the other hand, achieving good control over the functionality is virtually impossible with just kb + m. You can, if you feel like it, assign something like 10 buttons to the various stance controls of this game. To be fair, you can also do some very clever bindings with modifier keys and significantly cut down on the key binding requirement, including using a modifier key like ALT (holding ALT down) and using mouse movement (analog input!) to lean seamlessly and gain full control over your stances. The game features a really, really great stance system but to be perfectly honest, I never managed to get it working as intuitively and smoothly as I wanted. A leaning system in an FPS should be as intuitive and easy to use as using WASD for movement, anything more complex than that and it gets clumsy. Also, to be fair to ARMA's system, it's supposedly super incredible with head tracking equipment.

So yeah, you basically have simple systems like in STALKER with a simple Q/E button press which has the issue of lack of complexity, and you have super complex systems like ARMA which have the issue of being very hard to control quickly, easily and intuitively. It does feel like the right way for this mechanic is somewhere in the middle here, but hell if I know how that would translate to an actual concept.

Also, for multiplayer games specifically, the third person movement / animation implementation has to be taken into account as well, with lots of games that do have a leaning feature ending up with really awkward, twitchy animations for the leaning and all the problems associated with that. I think SWAT 3 / 4 are good examples of that, IIRC.

So I do disagree with the author's notion of "every FPS game should have this feature" because when it's implemented badly, it can bring along issues that wouldn't be there in absence of the feature. Beyond that I'm generally a huge fan of the concept, but I just haven't seen a 100% satisfying implementation of it so far.
